subject: Renal
vignette: A renal biopsy from a patient with nephritic-nephrotic syndrome shows glomeruli with increased mesangial cellularity and splitting of the glomerular basement membrane. On H&E and PAS stains, the capillary walls have a duplicated, 'tram-track' contour.
question: Which of the following best explains the tram-track appearance of the capillary walls?

options.text: Subepithelial immune-complex humps causing localized GBM spikes
Linear IgG deposition along a thickened GBM
Mesangial ingrowth with GBM splitting seen in membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Global podocyte foot-process effacement without GBM change
Crescent formation in Bowman space with fibrin and macrophages

explanation_correct: In membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, proliferation of mesangial cells and ingrowth into the capillary wall split the GBM into duplicated layers, producing the classic tram-track, or double-contour, appearance on H&E and PAS stains. This corresponds on electron microscopy to immune deposition and mesangial interposition. MPGN often presents with combined nephritic and nephrotic features, as in this patient.

explanation_incorrect.A: Subepithelial humps with GBM spike formation are the lesion of membranous nephropathy or post-streptococcal GN, not tram-tracking.
explanation_incorrect.B: Linear IgG along the GBM is the anti-GBM pattern of Goodpasture syndrome, not the duplicated GBM of MPGN.
explanation_incorrect.D: Diffuse foot-process effacement with a normal GBM is minimal change disease and does not create tram tracks.
explanation_incorrect.E: Crescents in Bowman space define rapidly progressive, crescentic GN, a different morphologic pattern from MPGN tram-tracking.

educationalObjective: MPGN produces tram-track capillary walls due to mesangial ingrowth and GBM splitting.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 40-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C presents with hematuria, proteinuria of 4 g/day, and renal insufficiency. Biopsy shows mesangial proliferation and tram-track GBM duplication. Immunofluorescence is granular, and electron microscopy demonstrates deposits on the subendothelial side of the GBM.
question: Which subtype of MPGN is most consistent with these findings and association?

options.text: Type II MPGN with C3 nephritic factor and intramembranous dense deposits
Type I MPGN with C3 nephritic factor and subepithelial humps
Type I MPGN, which may be secondary to HBV or HCV, with subendothelial immune-complex deposits
Type II MPGN associated with hepatitis B and subendothelial deposits
Lupus nephritis with wire loops and subendothelial IgG

explanation_correct: MPGN type I is the form that may be secondary to chronic infections, especially hepatitis B and hepatitis C. It is characterized by subendothelial immune-complex deposits with granular immunofluorescence and mesangial ingrowth producing tram-track GBM splitting. This patient's hepatitis C, subendothelial deposits, and tram-tracking fit type I MPGN.

explanation_incorrect.A: Type II MPGN is associated with C3 nephritic factor and has intramembranous dense deposits, not the subendothelial deposits seen here.
explanation_incorrect.B: C3 nephritic factor belongs to type II, and subepithelial humps are not the finding in type I MPGN.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hepatitis B is associated with type I, not type II, and type II features intramembranous rather than subendothelial deposits.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lupus nephritis shows wire-loop thickening with subendothelial IgG and C3 in the setting of SLE, not a hepatitis-associated tram-track lesion.

educationalObjective: MPGN type I may be secondary to HBV/HCV and shows subendothelial immune-complex deposits with tram-track GBM splitting.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 14-year-old girl has nephritic-nephrotic syndrome and persistently low serum C3 with normal C4. Renal biopsy shows tram-track GBM duplication. Immunofluorescence is positive for C3, and electron microscopy reveals dense deposits within the GBM itself, in an intramembranous location.
question: Which of the following best explains the persistent hypocomplementemia and renal findings?

options.text: Type I MPGN secondary to hepatitis C with subendothelial immune complexes
Type II MPGN, or dense deposit disease, with C3 nephritic factor stabilizing C3 convertase and causing persistent complement activation with low C3
Infection-related GN with consumptive hypocomplementemia and subepithelial humps
IgA nephropathy with mesangial IgA and normal complement
Minimal change disease with secondary complement activation

explanation_correct: MPGN type II, also called dense deposit disease, is associated with C3 nephritic factor, an IgG autoantibody that binds and stabilizes the alternative-pathway C3 convertase. This causes persistent complement activation and consumption, producing low C3 with relatively preserved C4. The deposits are intramembranous, distinguishing type II from type I's subendothelial deposits.

explanation_incorrect.A: Type I MPGN is associated with HBV and HCV and subendothelial deposits and is not driven by C3 nephritic factor with predominantly intramembranous deposits.
explanation_incorrect.C: Infection-related GN has subepithelial humps and hypocomplementemia following infection; it does not feature C3 nephritic factor or dense intramembranous deposits.
explanation_incorrect.D: IgA nephropathy features mesangial IgA deposition and typically normal complement, not low C3 with dense deposits.
explanation_incorrect.E: Minimal change disease is a podocyte disorder with normal complement and foot-process effacement, not complement consumption or dense deposits.

educationalObjective: MPGN type II (dense deposit disease) is driven by C3 nephritic factor causing persistent C3 activation, low C3, and intramembranous dense deposits.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 30-year-old woman has 6 g/day proteinuria, edema, microscopic hematuria with RBC casts, and creatinine 1.9 mg/dL. Biopsy shows hypercellular glomeruli with tram-track GBM splitting and granular immunofluorescence; electron microscopy localizes the deposits. The clinician notes that her presentation combines nephrotic and nephritic features.
question: Which of the following best characterizes MPGN as a cause of this presentation?

options.text: It is a purely nephrotic disease caused by podocyte injury with foot-process effacement
It is a purely nephritic disease with subnephrotic proteinuria and no edema
It is always secondary to systemic lupus erythematosus with wire-loop deposits
It often presents as nephritic-nephrotic syndrome, with type I showing subendothelial and type II intramembranous deposits
It is characterized by linear anti-GBM IgG and pulmonary hemorrhage

explanation_correct: MPGN, together with DPGN, is one of the most common causes of nephritic-nephrotic syndrome, in which nephrotic-range proteinuria coexists with nephritic features such as hematuria, RBC casts, and renal insufficiency. Type I shows subendothelial immune-complex deposits and may be secondary to HBV or HCV; type II shows intramembranous dense deposits with C3 nephritic factor. Both show granular immunofluorescence and tram-track GBM splitting.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pure nephrotic disease from podocyte injury describes minimal change disease or other primary nephrotic causes, not the proliferative inflammatory lesion of MPGN.
explanation_incorrect.B: MPGN is not purely nephritic with subnephrotic proteinuria; it commonly produces nephrotic-range proteinuria with edema.
explanation_incorrect.C: MPGN is not always secondary to SLE; only DPGN is classically lupus associated, whereas MPGN may be primary or related to infection and complement dysregulation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Linear anti-GBM IgG with pulmonary hemorrhage describes Goodpasture syndrome, not the granular tram-track lesion of MPGN.

educationalObjective: MPGN commonly causes nephritic-nephrotic syndrome; type I has subendothelial deposits (HBV/HCV), type II has intramembranous dense deposits (C3 nephritic factor).
